title: Longest Cycle in a Graph
statement:
A directed graph has `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1`, and every node has at most one outgoing edge. The array `edges` (length `n`) describes it: when `edges[i]` is not `-1` there is an edge from node `i` to node `edges[i]`, and `edges[i] == -1` means node `i` has no outgoing edge.

A cycle is a path that leaves some node and eventually comes back to that same node; its length is the number of edges (equivalently, distinct nodes) on it. Return the length of the longest cycle in the graph, or `-1` if the graph has no cycle at all.
notes:
## Intuition

Because each node has at most one outgoing edge, starting anywhere and following edges traces a single path: it either stops at a `-1` or runs into a loop. Every node lies on at most one cycle, so the graph splits into a few cycles with trees of paths draining into them. A brute force follows edges from every node until it comes back (O(n²)); a single DFS-style sweep that stamps each node with the time it was reached finds every cycle while visiting each node once.

## Approach

1. Keep `visitedAt[node]` (0 means never reached) and a global `clock` that grows by one per visited node.
2. For each `start` not yet visited, remember `walkStart = clock` and walk `node = edges[node]`, stamping each fresh node with the clock.
3. The walk stops at `-1` or at a node that already has a stamp.
4. If that node was stamped during this walk (`visitedAt[node] >= walkStart`), the walk just closed a cycle; its length is `clock - visitedAt[node]`. Update `longest`.
5. A stamp from an earlier walk means this path drains into territory already explored, so no new cycle.

## Example 1, step by step

`edges = [3,3,4,2,3]`. From `start = 0`: node 0 gets time 1, node 3 time 2, node 2 time 3, node 4 time 4; the next node is 3, stamped at 2 which is at least `walkStart = 1`. `clock` is now 5, so the cycle length is `5 - 2 = 3`. From `start = 1`: node 1 gets time 5 and leads to 3, stamped at 2, below `walkStart = 5`, so nothing new. The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): every node is stamped once and each walk step stamps a node.
- Space: O(n) for `visitedAt`.

## Pitfalls

- Reaching an already stamped node does not always mean a cycle; only stamps from the current walk do.
- Do not reset the visited marks between starts, or the work becomes O(n²).
- Return `-1` (not `0`) when no cycle exists.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `visitedAt` | time each node was first reached, 0 if never |
| `clock` | the next time stamp to hand out |
| `longest` | longest cycle length found so far |
| `start` | the node a new walk begins from |
| `walkStart` | first time stamp used by the current walk |
| `node` | the node the walk is currently at |

narration.3: visitedAt holds the time each node was first reached; 0 marks a node no walk has touched yet.
narration.4: The clock starts at 1 so that a stamp of 0 can mean unvisited.
narration.5: No cycle has been found yet, so the answer starts at -1.
narration.7: Try every node as the beginning of a new walk.
narration.8: A node already stamped belongs to an earlier walk, so walking from it again finds nothing new.
narration.11: Remember the first stamp this walk will hand out, to tell its own nodes from older ones.
narration.13: Keep following edges while there is an edge and the next node is still unvisited.
narration.14: Stamp the current node with the current time.
narration.18: The walk stopped at a node stamped during this same walk, so it closed a cycle.
narration.19: The cycle runs from that node's stamp up to the current clock; keep the longest length.
narration.22: Every node has been visited once; return the longest cycle, or -1 if none.
